> **Cons 1. The biggest problem of this work is that the extreme imaging condition only works for the RGB camera but not for the event stream. According to Fig. 1, the low-light/blur effect is only added by the setting configurations for the RGB camera, while the signal to the event camera is not in low-light/blur condition. So, if I'm not wrong, the discussion of this paper that "tackle pose estimation and tracking in extreme conditions by leveraging the advantages of the event camera" is based on a wrong assumption or an unproperly constructed dataset.**

**Response:** We sincerely apologize for any misunderstanding. We would like to clarify that there were some inaccuracies in the reviewer's understanding. In our triplet camera system, both the event camera and the degraded RGB camera experienced the same degradation effects.

**• Low-light Degradation**

In Fig. 1, we used an ND filter for the RGB camera to handle low-light and/or blur conditions, and we applied the same ND filter to the event camera to match the light levels exactly. We also used identical lenses for both the RGB and event cameras, ensuring that the aperture settings were the same to apply the degradation effects uniformly. While the event camera performs robustly in low-light conditions due to its lower low-light cutoff [A, B], it does experience some degradation where the event data edges become blunt and suppressed in very low-light environments. For example, in the extreme low-light conditions shown in the second row of Fig. 6, the event data shows more suppression and blurred edges compared to the data in the first row.

**• Blur Effects**

The event camera operates asynchronously and does not have a separate exposure time; its temporal resolution is over 10,000 FPS, which inherently prevents motion blur. Since we streamed and acquired data from the event camera continuously without a separate exposure time, it experienced the same motion effects as the other cameras.

We will clarify this aspect to emphasize that both the RGB and event cameras experienced the same level of degradation, ensuring that there is no misunderstanding.

[A] Towards Robust Event-guided Low-Light Image Enhancement: A Large-Scale Real-World Event-Image Dataset and Novel Approach, CVPR 2024

[B] Coherent Event Guided Low-Light Video Enhancement, ICCV 2023

> **Cons 2. I don't think the discussion of the benchmark experiment leads to a very meaningful conclusion or discovery for this community. Using an event stream to augment the performance of HPE under extreme imaging conditions is a well-explored idea.**

**Response:** We would like to emphasize the unique aspects of our dataset. Our research is the first to use event streams for human pose estimation (HPE) under extreme conditions. 
Although there are cases where events have been used in HPE research, there are no examples that effectively utilize the advantages of events in extreme motion blur situations and low light conditions, such as high temporal resolution and the ability to capture scene details well in low light.
While there have been studies using events for HPE, none have highlighted the strengths of events in low-light cutoff and high temporal resolution. 
We demonstrated the feasibility of performing HPE in environments with low light and motion blur using a multi-modal event-RGB setup.

Although there are studies [17, 18, 40] that perform HPE in blurred environments using only RGB, these studies generated blur synthetically, which differs significantly from real blur [19, 41, 42]. Therefore, leveraging the features of events to conduct multi-modal research in real blur and low-light environments is sufficiently novel. Our study showcases the strengths of event cameras in extreme conditions, and this benchmark can serve as a valuable dataset for achieving better performance in future research.

> **Q5. What are the resolutions of RGB camera and event camera respectively, and how to align images with different camera resolutions?**

**Response:** As mentioned in Table 1, the final resolution for both the RGB and event cameras is 1373$\times$928. To geometrically align the two different cameras, we used a beam splitter. The beam splitter allows the same light to pass through both cameras, making their baseline nearly zero. Any remaining minor baseline issues and resolution discrepancies were precisely aligned using global homography, with detailed methods described in previous work [L].

[L] Time Lens++: Event-based Frame Interpolation with Parametric Non-linear Flow and Multi-scale Fusion, CVPR 2022

> **Q6. The motion blur in this article is artificially created by increasing the exposure time, and the motion itself does not produce a particularly large motion blur.**

**Response:** In response to comment 3, we also note that, as shown in the table, we have captured many sports scenarios. For these scenes, the exposure time for the blur camera was under 60 ms, with an FPS of approximately 20. This value is not significantly different from most camera FPS and does not represent an artificially extended scenario compared to real conditions. In other words, the blur camera was used in situations with substantial actual scene or camera motion, not in artificially prolonged settings.

> **Q7. Another camera can still record images that are clear enough to annotate the ground truth.**

**Response:** To achieve clear images, we set the exposure time of another camera to be very short. We also chose locations and times with excellent lighting conditions to capture well-lit and sharp images. However, in typical situations, insufficient lighting may result in low-light images, or there may be a need to increase the exposure time to obtain sharp images, which can lead to severe blur when motion is present. Especially in low-light environments, increasing the exposure time further exacerbates the blur, making it difficult to achieve the sharpness seen with the camera used for the ground truth data.

> **Q8. How can such a large motion blur occur in reality? Under what conditions is it necessary to perform human pose estimation and tracking in low light and motion blur?**

**Response:** Large motion blur can occur in many real scenarios: 1) when the camera is moving rapidly, 2) when the subject's motion is extremely fast, or 3) when both conditions are present simultaneously. 

In the first case, situations such as estimating and tracking human poses in autonomous vehicles or fast-moving robots can lead to significant motion blur due to rapid camera movement. As mentioned in [M], to achieve precise autonomous driving, it is essential to understand human motion in the driving scene; the motion blur can hinder human recognition and tracking in autonomous driving scenarios. 
Additionally, autonomous vehicles can operate at night, and in such situations, due to the lack of ambient light, we often increase the exposure time to capture images. However, this extended exposure time can lead to significant motion blur.

For the second and third cases, consider scenarios like sports, where capturing very fast-moving subjects with a tracking camera can lead to severe blur. In sports scenarios, capturing subjects in low-light conditions is also common, further exacerbating the problem of large motion blur. Therefore, research on human perception under large motion blur and low-light conditions is crucial.

In fact, when we captured data, we recorded it at nearly 20 FPS, but since the subject was moving quickly and we followed the subject while filming, severe motion blur occurred. This demonstrates that motion blur can easily happen in real-world scenarios.

[M] Scalability in Perception for Autonomous Driving: Waymo Open Dataset, CVPR2020

> **Comment 5. There are many deblurring methods based on RGB images now, so why use event cameras?**

**Response:** Recent studies on deblurring using event cameras [E, F] show that these event-guided methods significantly outperform traditional RGB camera-based approaches. Specifically, when both the camera and the subject are moving, traditional RGB-based deblurring methods often perform poorly, while event cameras have proven robust in such environments. Building on this existing research, our study is motivated to use event cameras to achieve the final end-task human pose estimation without requiring deblurring.

**Response:**  As seen in existing event datasets, background data from event cameras is often treated as natural noise and is not processed further. > **Comment 1.  Manual annotation errors.**

**Response:** Our triple-axis camera system is designed to perform labeling even in extreme scenarios, such as low-light conditions or situations with severe motion blur. One of the RGB cameras was used as a reference for labeling, as it was captured with a short exposure time and under well-lit conditions to ensure higher accuracy in manual annotation. Additionally, to minimize errors during the annotation process, multiple annotators conducted cross-checks to achieve the most precise labeling possible. The sample data we provided demonstrates that we have ensured accurate labeling.

> **Comment 2.  Provide only 2D information and annotations.**

**Response:** The goal of our dataset is to estimate "multi" human poses in extreme environments. These extreme scenarios include situations commonly encountered in everyday life, such as sports scenarios, rapid camera motion, low-light conditions, and severe motion blur. Previous studies have obtained 3D information by attaching sensors to individuals, but this approach has limitations, especially when dealing with multiple people and spatial constraints. Therefore, due to these limitations, we have acquired our dataset using 2D data. Based on this research, we plan to pursue the acquisition of 3D motion as future work.

> **Comment 3.  The motion blur is artificially induced by longer exposure, while the actual motion causes minimal blur; another camera still captures clear images for ground truth annotation.**

**Response:** According to existing researches [A,B,C] exploring motion blur in real-world scenarios, our approach is not artificial.
Real blurred images are generated through the integral of the signal from photons detected by the sensor, and the blur image is created through signal accumulation. 
When the camera sensor receives the signal $S(t)$ over an exposure time $\tau$, the blurred image $I_b$ is formulated as follows:
$I_b = \int_0^\tau S(t) \, dt \quad $.
According to this formulation, the camera used to capture the paired sharp image is set to a shorter exposure time to minimize the effects of blur. On the other hand, a blurred image results from allowing a sufficiently long exposure time, which creates motion blur during that period. Acquiring data from the same scene using different exposure times simultaneously is referred to as a real-world blur dataset [A, B, C]. Deblurring models trained on paired blur and sharp images obtained through this process have been shown to perform well on real blur images. In other words, it is important to emphasize that the blurred images captured from our triple-axis are not synthetic but real-world blur images generated from actual motion. Moreover, in the sports scene shown in Fig. 2, significant blur is observed due to the motion of the object alone, even without a large exposure time. 

As noted by the reviewer, sharp images can be captured with short exposure times under bright lighting conditions, but this becomes difficult in many situations, including low-light conditions. To overcome this, the camera's exposure time must be increased, significantly increasing the blur effect. Therefore, it is not always true that a camera with a short exposure time will capture clean images.  In practice, to avoid situations where increasing the exposure could cause blur in the sharp camera during data collection, we gathered data under bright lighting conditions.


[A] Real-world video deblurring: A benchmark dataset and an efficient recurrent neural network, IJCV 2023

[B] Real-World Blur Dataset for Learning and Benchmarking Deblurring Algorithms, ECCV 2020

[C] Blur Interpolation Transformer for Real-World Motion from Blur, CVPR 2023

> **Comment 4.  The motivation behind this article is not clear enough. What is the practical application of this work? How could such a large motion blur occur in reality?**

**Response:** As mentioned in the introduction of the main paper, human motion is dynamic, and the time and location of activities vary greatly. A significant portion of human pose datasets is used in sports, where dynamic motion frequently occurs. For instance, the PoseTrack21 [6] dataset often contains blurred images, even captured by high-quality cameras during sports.

Our goal is to expand the application of human pose estimation using multi-modal sensors. In practice, sports videos frequently naturally exhibit blur. Additionally, human activities can occur at all times, including low-light conditions such as early evening or night, where perception might require increased exposure time, potentially resulting in severe blur [D].

[D] LEDNet: Joint Low-light Enhancement and Deblurring in the Dark.

We understand the reviewer's concerns; however, we would like to emphasize the following strengths and potential applications of our dataset:

• Interest in research focused on estimating human poses in the presence of motion blur has been steadily increasing [17, 18, 40]. Previous studies have synthesized blur due to the lack of a real blurred human pose dataset, which results in significant differences from real-world blur [19, 41, 42]. In contrast, our dataset is generated using real-world blur and can be effectively utilized for research focused solely on RGB data, even without being multi-modal. Additionally, the presence of low-light conditions, which are closely related to blur, further highlights the uniqueness of our dataset.

• We also want to highlight the growing attention within the research community towards event camera studies. Event cameras are being increasingly researched at major conferences every year (e.g., 40 papers at CVPR 2024, 5 at NeurIPS 2023, 23 at ICCV 2023, and more than 3 at ICLR 2024), and this number continues to rise. Event cameras are particularly effective in addressing challenges that are difficult to solve with conventional RGB-based cameras. Currently, there is no multi-person pose dataset collected using event cameras, and the fact that it was captured in extreme conditions further enhances the value of the dataset. We have particularly highlighted the advantages of event cameras in extreme conditions (e.g., motion blur and low-light conditions), and we believe that this dataset will serve as a foundation for many future studies. While the price of these cameras might seem relatively high at the moment, given the current trends in the community, we anticipate that the value of these cameras will continue to increase, which will likely lead to a decrease in their cost over time.

summary_and_contributions.value:
# Summary
The paper introduces a new dataset with RGB and event stream for 2D human pose estimation and tracking in the extreme scenarios of low-light and motion blur environments. Several baseline methods are examined on this dataset to build a benchmark.

# Contributions
1. The author has built a triplet camera system with RGB and event cameras for extreme imaging conditioning and annotation.
2. To the best of my knowledge, it's the first dataset for multi-human 2D pose estimation and tracking with RGB and real events.
3. The dataset is captured in different environments and seems to cover more diverse poses than existing related works.

review.value:
# Pros.
1. The paper is well written.
2. The design of the triplet camera system is novel to me.
3. The paper provides some statistical analysis of the dataset and its counterparts.

# Cons.
1. The biggest problem of this work is that the extreme imaging condition only works for the RGB camera but not for the event stream. According to Fig. 1, the low-light/blur effect is only added by the setting configurations for the RGB camera, while the signal to the event camera is not in low-light/blur condition. So, if I'm not wrong, the discussion of this paper that "tackle pose estimation and tracking in extreme conditions by leveraging the advantages of the event camera" is based on a wrong assumption or an unproperly constructed dataset.
2. I don't think the discussion of the benchmark experiment leads to a very meaningful conclusion or discovery for this community. Using event stream to augment the performance of HPE under extreme imaging conditions is a well-explored idea. Moreover, the discussion is not very related to the multi-human setting.
3. The baseline methods for 2D HPE are not very new.

summary_and_contributions.value:
* The paper proposes Event-guided Human Pose Estimation and Tracking in extreme conditions dataset (e.g., motion blur and low-light scenarios), using a new type modality, which is event camera.
* The EHPT-XC dataset firstly proposes event or event+RGB-based human pose estimation dataset, specifically in multi-human scenarios.

review.value:
The paper proposes the first dataset for event-camera-based human pose estimation specifically in multi-human scenarios, which can widely be used for future research for HPE under extreme conditions. The motivation of introducing new modality as well as the novelty of the dataset looks persuasive to me. Despite this, I have some comments for further improving the quality of the paper & dataset.

- Wireless signals (e.g., WiFi or mmWave radar) can effectively resolve the problem of low-light pose estimation with their inherent resilience on light variation. It would be great to include wireless-based pose datasets in Table 1 and add related discussions as well, to place the proposed work compared to them too.
- It would be great if the authors have the Event-only-based pose estimation outcomes quantitatively or qualitatively for better comparison among RGB vs Event vs RGB+Event.
- It is recommended to provide the processing code as well for better reproduction of the data.

strengths.value:
- The paper is written well.
- Motivation of introducing event camera for blurry & low-lighting scenarios looks clear.
- The paper firstly proposes the event camera-based human pose estimation & tracking dataset, which can be effectively utilized for future research.

title.value: A Benchmark Dataset for Event-Guided Human Pose Estimation and Tracking in Extreme Conditions

abstract.value:
Multi-person pose estimation and tracking have been actively researched by the computer vision community due to their practical applicability. However, existing human pose estimation and tracking datasets have only been successful in typical scenarios, such as those without motion blur or with well-lit conditions. These RGB-based datasets are limited to learning under extreme motion blur situations or poor lighting conditions, making them inherently vulnerable to such scenarios.
As a promising solution, bio-inspired event cameras exhibit robustness in extreme scenarios due to their high dynamic range and micro-second level temporal resolution. Therefore, in this paper, we introduce a new hybrid dataset encompassing both RGB and event data for human pose estimation and tracking in two extreme scenarios: low-light and motion blur environments. The proposed Event-guided Human Pose Estimation and Tracking in eXtreme Conditions (EHPT-XC) dataset covers cases of motion blur caused by dynamic objects and low-light conditions individually as well as both simultaneously. With EHPT-XC, we aim to inspire researchers to tackle pose estimation and tracking in extreme conditions by leveraging the advantageous of the event camera. Project pages are available at https://github.com/Chohoonhee/EHPT-XC.

    submissions = client.get_all_notes(content= { 'venueid': submission_venue_id })
    print(f'update {len(submissions)} submissions')
    openreview.tools.concurrent_requests(post_submission_edit, submissions, desc='post_submission_edit')
